blocks.text: A danfo leaves Oshodi, drives 6 km east to Ikeja, then turns round and drives 6 km back. The odometer says it covered 12 km, but the bus is exactly where it started. Distance and displacement are genuinely different quantities, and mixing them up is the first place marks are lost in motion questions.

blocks.markdown:
**Distance** is the total path length travelled — a scalar, so it only has size. **Displacement** is the straight-line change in position *in a stated direction* — a vector.

In the same way, **speed** is distance ÷ time (scalar) while **velocity** is displacement ÷ time (vector). The danfo above had an average speed of something real, but an average velocity of zero, because its displacement was zero.

blocks.title: Acceleration
blocks.text: The rate of change of velocity with time, measured in metres per second squared (m s⁻²). Because velocity is a vector, acceleration occurs whenever speed changes, direction changes, or both. A negative acceleration in the direction of travel is called retardation or deceleration.

blocks.caption: Acceleration from a change in velocity, where u is initial and v is final velocity

blocks.markdown:
### The equations of uniformly accelerated motion

When the acceleration is **constant**, four equations link the five quantities $u$, $v$, $a$, $s$ and $t$. Each equation leaves out exactly one of them, so you pick the equation that omits the quantity you neither know nor want.

rows: You know time and want the final velocity
You know time and want the distance
Time is neither given nor wanted
You know both velocities and the time
blocks.caption: The four equations of motion. They apply ONLY to uniform (constant) acceleration.

blocks.title: A car accelerating from rest
blocks.prompt: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2.5 m/s² for 8.0 s. Calculate (a) its final velocity and (b) the distance it covers.

steps.text: List what you know. Starting from rest means the initial velocity is zero.
For part (a), the equation that omits distance is v = u + at.
Evaluate the final velocity, with units.
For part (b), use the equation that omits final velocity.
Substitute, remembering that the first term vanishes because u = 0.

blocks.markdown:
### Motion under gravity

A freely falling body has a constant downward acceleration $g$. In WAEC, NECO and JAMB questions **take $g = 10\ \text{m}\,\text{s}^{-2}$** unless the paper tells you otherwise.

The same four equations apply — just replace $a$ with $g$ and be careful with signs. Taking downwards as positive for a falling body keeps everything positive:

$$v = gt, \qquad h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^{2}, \qquad v^{2} = 2gh$$

For a body thrown **upwards** with initial speed $u$, gravity opposes the motion, so $a = -g$. At the highest point $v = 0$, which gives the two standard results $H = \frac{u^{2}}{2g}$ for maximum height and $t = \frac{u}{g}$ for time to reach it.

blocks.title: A stone dropped from a bridge
blocks.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest from a bridge 45 m above a river. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the time it takes to reach the water and its speed on impact.

steps.text: Dropped from rest, so the initial velocity is zero and the acceleration is g downwards.
Use the equation linking height, acceleration and time.
Make t² the subject and take the square root.
For the impact speed use v = gt.

blocks.answer: t = 3 s and the impact speed is 30 m/s downwards

blocks.title: Mass does not appear
blocks.text: Neither the time of fall nor the impact speed depends on the mass of the object. A 2 kg stone and a 20 kg stone dropped together from the same height land together, because g is the same for both. Air resistance, not mass, is what makes a feather fall slowly.

blocks.title: WAEC and JAMB tip
blocks.text: Before substituting, write out u, v, a, s and t in a column and fill in what you are given. The equation you need is the one containing the three knowns plus the unknown. This takes fifteen seconds and eliminates almost all wrong-equation errors.

points: Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are vectors that require a direction.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = (v − u) ÷ t, in m s⁻².
The four equations of motion apply only when acceleration is uniform: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as and s = ½(u + v)t.
For free fall take g = 10 m s⁻² in Nigerian exams: v = gt, h = ½gt² and v² = 2gh.
For a body projected upwards, maximum height is u²/2g and the time to reach it is u/g; total time of flight back to the start is 2u/g.
